title: A Cheat-Sensitive Primitive for Destination-Private Quantum Routing
authors: S. F. E. Oliviero, S. Onofri, V. Giovannetti
abstract: Quantum networks will rely on intermediate nodes to distribute entanglement, but the same nodes may learn which users are being connected. We introduce a minimal two-call routing primitive in which a user, Alice, establishes an entangled link with one of several clients while testing whether the provider, Bob, has disturbed a coherently encoded request. The construction adapts the hidden-order mechanism of quantum private queries: one call contains a direct request, the other a coherent superposition of the desired and null addresses, and Alice keeps their order secret. A private matching qubit held by the selected client restores the coherent test state after a favorable Bell-measurement outcome, so that Alice can test the returned query without any further operation by Bob. The claim is deliberately limited. The protocol shows that a routing request can carry a physical cheating test, and it detects an explicit destination-reading attack with nonzero probability. It does not yet provide a quantitative information-disturbance tradeoff, composable security, or certification of an unmeasured output against arbitrary attacks. We also characterize the exact perfect-pass limit, in which Bob's residual state, averaged over the private matching states, is independent of the destination.
summary: This paper introduces a minimal two-call quantum routing primitive designed to test for eavesdropping on the destination address in quantum networks. By combining a direct request with a coherent 'trap' call, the protocol achieves a cheat-sensitive test that detects reading attacks. The work establishes strong privacy guarantees in the perfect-pass limit, advancing the theory of secure quantum communication.
main_problem: To develop a minimal quantum routing primitive that allows a user to establish an entangled link while simultaneously testing whether an intermediate provider has read the destination address.
main_result: The protocol is shown to be 'cheat-sensitive,' detecting explicit destination-reading attacks with non-zero probability, and achieving destination privacy in the 'perfect-pass limit.'
method: The methodology adapts the hidden-order mechanism from Quantum Private Queries, utilizing a two-call structure involving a direct request and a coherent superposition 'trap' call.
model_or_system: The model is a star-network quantum routing setup involving a user (Alice), a provider (Bob), and multiple clients. It relies on shared entangled singlets and private matching qubits held by the clients.
key_observables: Detection probability of an attack, Bob's residual state, and the state's dependence on the destination address $j$.
important_parameters: The protocol is limited to a two-call primitive, and the analysis characterizes the 'perfect-pass limit' where the residual state is independent of the destination.
main_assumptions: The claim is deliberately limited; it does not provide a quantitative information-disturbance tradeoff or composable security. The perfect-pass limit assumes ideal initial singlets and exact direct functionality.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the star-network implementation, detailing the roles of Alice, Bob, the clients, the singlets, and the private matching qubit $Q(j)$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the two-call protocol, analyzing the state evolution after favorable Bell outcomes, deriving the detection probability for attacks, and finally proving the strong privacy guarantee by showing the residual state is destination-independent in the perfect-pass limit.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum networking primitives, the rigorous analysis of information leakage and privacy guarantees in a controlled quantum channel setting provides foundational theoretical tools applicable to understanding information flow in complex quantum systems.
